The workshop's case studies were chosen from the work of SCORE, a research programme that tested the claims of published social and behavioural research in three different ways, and the exercise that each case study teaches repeats on a small scale the design of the SCORE robustness study [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness], in which other analysts reanalysed the data behind those claims. This page describes the programme and its three studies, the way in which the robustness study chose its claims and organised the work of its analysts, how it made their results comparable and what its article reports, and what the record of the programme holds for each case study.

## The programme {#sec-score}

SCORE, short for Systematizing Confidence in Open Research and Evidence, was a programme funded by DARPA, the research agency of the United States Department of Defense, which put claims from published social and behavioural research through three kinds of repetition [@AlipourfardEtAl2021SystematizingConfidenceOpen]. A reproduction repeats the original analysis on the original data, a robustness check applies different but defensible analyses to the same data, and a replication asks the same question of new data. The three studies, which were reported together in *Nature* in 2026, shared one sampling frame, for which "a stratified random sample of 600 articles was identified from a larger pool of approximately 30,000 randomly stratified articles across 62 journals published between 2009 and 2018" [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, Methods], and in each article the central claim was traced from the abstract to the statistical result that supports it.

The SCORE reproducibility study asked the authors of the 600 papers for their data and code [@MiskeEtAl2026InvestigatingReproducibilitySocial]. The authors of 144 papers (24.0%) made their data available, and the team rebuilt the datasets of 38 others from source data, so that 182 datasets were in hand, of which 143 were assessed. Of these papers, 53.6% were rated as precisely reproducible and 73.5% as at least approximately reproducible, that is, "within 15% of the original effects or within 0.05 of original P values" [@MiskeEtAl2026InvestigatingReproducibilitySocial, p. 126]. Reproducibility was higher in political science and economics than in the other fields, in more recent papers, and in papers from journals that require their authors to share data (p. 126).

The SCORE replicability study tested 274 claims of positive results from 164 quantitative papers, published in 54 of the journals, with replications that had a median power of 99.6% to detect the original effect size [@TynerEtAl2026InvestigatingReplicabilitySocial, p. 143]. The replications showed a statistically significant result in the original pattern for 151 of the 274 claims (55.1%), and the median effect size, as a Pearson correlation, fell from 0.25 in the original studies to 0.10 in the replications. Whether a replication succeeds is itself a matter of method, since the thirteen ways of judging success that the study applied gave rates from 28.6% to 74.8% (p. 143).

The robustness study [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness] is the subject of the rest of this page.

## The robustness study {#sec-robustness}

### The design {#sec-design}

The robustness study is also known as Multi100, the name under which its records are kept on the OSF and its code on GitHub. The study set out to measure how far published conclusions and results depend on the choices of the analyst who produced them. Its preregistration gives the main aim as "to estimate the degree to which published conclusions and results in social and behavioural sciences are robust to the analytical choices of analysts", and it asks two questions: "Do different analysts arrive at the same conclusions as the analyst of the original study? Do different analysts arrive at the same effect estimates (+/- 0.05 Cohen's d) as the analyst of the original study?" ([osf.io/4ev9t](https://osf.io/4ev9t), p. 2).

The claims came from the first phase of SCORE, in which a single claim had been extracted from the abstract of each article, one that "ideally corresponded to one statistically significant inferential test result" (preregistration, p. 5). The lead team of the robustness study kept the claims that were understandable, contained only one claim, indicated the direction of the effect and had a test in the article that corresponded to them (p. 5), and where it judged an expression of a claim "ambiguous or rhetorical", it replaced the expression with an ellipsis "while preserving the original wording and the meaning of the claim" (p. 5). The ellipses in the claims of the case studies come from this step. The published Methods add that each selected study had to contain "a single inferential statistical test result that corresponded to the claim with our instructions" [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, Methods].

Each claim went to at least five analysts, who worked independently with the data of the original study and with the full article in hand, since the lead team "opted for complete transparency of the original article so that no potentially important information is missing for the co-analyst" (preregistration, p. 4). The analysts received the claim but no research question, as the preregistration states: "We will provide the co-analysts with the above described claims to test on the original datasets but we will not give them specific research questions" (p. 5). In all, 457 analysts produced 504 reanalyses of 100 studies [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, p. 136], and Chris Moreh, who leads this workshop, was one of the analysts.

The work came in two tasks. In the first, the analysts could "conduct and report as many analyses as they wish but they will have to draw a single conclusion from their analysis" (preregistration, p. 7), choosing between evidence for the claim, evidence for the opposite effect, evidence neither way and evidence for the null hypothesis (p. 8). In the second, each analyst produced "only one statistical result corresponding to the claim they studied in Task 1, which will be compared to a statistical result in the original paper", under instructions of the lead team on matters such as "data selection, exclusions" (p. 7). The published Methods explain why both tasks were needed, the first answering the question about conclusions and the second the question about effect estimates, since "asking only one of the tasks would not have been sufficient to fully address both questions" [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, Methods], and a panel of peers then judged whether each analysis was appropriate.

The instruction of the second task is where the background page of each case study picks up the story, because the instruction settled some of the decisions that the five analysts of the case study faced and left others to the analysts. Much of the spread among the five results of a case study arguably comes from the decisions that the instruction left open.

### A common scale {#sec-scale}

The results of the robustness study appeared in *Nature* in 2026, in an article that reports two kinds of agreement between the 504 reanalyses and the 100 original studies: whether the analysts reached the same conclusion as the original authors, which the first task recorded, and whether they arrived at the same effect size, which came from the second. The five analysts of one claim seldom report the same kind of statistic, since one may fit a regression and report the t of its coefficient, another run a chi-square test on a table, and a third report the z of a mixed model fitted to respondents. The article states the problem, and the solution that it chose, in one passage:

> A challenge in any multi-analyst project is to find a common metric that allows the results of the different analyses to be compared. A practical solution is to transform the reported point estimates into a standard effect-size measure. Although these transformations have limitations and their calculation relies on assumptions that may not hold in all considered analysis settings, for the sake of comparability, we decided to compute Cohen's d for each reanalysis, wherever it was feasible. [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, p. 136]

The conversion ran in two steps in the code published by the project, which first turned each reported statistic into a correlation r and then turned r into Cohen's d, as $d = 2r / \sqrt{1 - r^2}$. The first step takes a different rule for each family of statistics, and each rule needs a second number besides the statistic itself:

| Reported statistic | Rule of the code, as a formula | The number that enters beside the statistic |
|:--|:--|:--|
| t | $r = t / \sqrt{t^2 + df}$ | the degrees of freedom, as reported |
| z | $r = \tanh\left(\lvert z \rvert / \sqrt{N - 3}\right)$, with the sign of z | the sample size N |
| $\chi^2$ | $r = \tanh\left(\sqrt{\chi^2} / \sqrt{N - 3}\right)$, which is never negative | the sample size N |
| F | $r = \sqrt{F / (F + df_2)}$ | the second degrees of freedom |
| r | taken as it is | – |

: The rules of `standard_correlation_coefficient.R` and `cohens_d.R`, in the repository of the team of the robustness study at [github.com/marton-balazs-kovacs/multi100](https://github.com/marton-balazs-kovacs/multi100). {.striped}

The direction of each result was then set by a convention of the project: "All original effect sizes are reported as positive values, whereas the reanalysis effect sizes are negative only when they indicate an opposite effect compared with the original study" [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, Methods]. The sign of a reanalysis in the record therefore states its direction relative to the claim, as the analyst reported that direction in the second task, rather than the sign of the estimate itself. In the Europeanisation and the economy case study, one analyst whose estimate ran in the direction of the claim ticked the opposite direction, and the effect size of that reanalysis entered the record with a negative sign.

### What the conversion assumes {#sec-assumptions}

The rules for t, z and $\chi^2$ arguably treat the number that enters them as the number of independent units that carry the evidence. The rule for z, for instance, inverts the test of a simple correlation on N independent observations. That number weighs on the result as much as the statistic does, and it depends on what the software of each analyst counted. In the Europeanisation case study, two analysts reported almost the same statistic, z = −3.59 and t = −3.80, yet the correlations recorded for them differ by a factor of about 42, at −0.006 and −0.242, because the z was converted on the 394,575 respondents of its analysis and the t on the 233 degrees of freedom of a model fitted to country-years. Neither number is wrong for its own model, and the difference comes from the conversion, which reads the units that the software counted as the units that the claim is about, and for a predictor that varies between countries and years, such as the national unemployment rate of that case study, counting every respondent as an independent test of a country-level quantity may well be too strong an assumption.

The comparison with the original study is made on d, within a tolerance region that the preregistration set and justified:

> We will regard a new result to be different from the original one if its effect size is beyond the +/-0.05 Cohen's d tolerance region of the original result (carefully considering the direction of the effect in each analysis). We decided to use this method instead of simply checking whether the effect size estimates are significantly different, because Cohen's ds are independent of sample size, and that way, we will allow the same analytical variability for studies with small sample size as with large sample size. ([osf.io/4ev9t](https://osf.io/4ev9t), p. 9)

Confidence intervals were set aside on purpose, because "this assessment would be misleading as less precise estimates (greater CIs) would appear more robust" (preregistration, p. 9). The article keeps the preregistered region of ±0.05 d and adds analyses with wider regions, ±0.20 d among them [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, p. 136]. The independence of d from the sample size holds within a fixed design, however, and across analyses that count different units for the same predictor, as in the example above, the same region is in effect wider for some analyses than for others.

### What the article found {#sec-findings}

The article reports first that analysts who worked on the same data seldom produced the same numbers: "in 81% of the studies, the corresponding analysts reported different statistics about statistical test families (such as t-tests, F-tests and $\chi^2$ tests) and their values (after rounding them to two decimal places)" [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, p. 136]. On the common scale, "in 5% (5 out of 95) of the studies for which we could obtain the original effect size, all reanalysis effect sizes were inside the tolerance region (±0.05 Cohen's d) of the result of the original study", and "[o]f the 396 available reanalysis effect sizes, 34% were inside the tolerance region" (p. 136). With the region of ±0.20 d, all the reanalyses of a study fell inside it in 23% of the studies, as did 57% of the reanalysis effect sizes (p. 136). The effects also tended to be smaller on reanalysis, with a mean d of 0.73 in the original studies against 0.49 in the reanalyses, and medians of 0.43 and 0.35 (p. 138).

The conclusions held up better than the effect sizes. "Across all individual reanalyses (n = 504), 74% of analyses arrived at the same conclusion as the original investigation, 24% yielded no effects or inconclusive results and 2% indicated an effect in the opposite direction from the original investigation" (p. 138). Of the 100 claims, 34% were robust in the strict sense that every analyst reported evidence for the claim, a share that depends on how much agreement the definition asks for, since it rises to 39% when more than 80% of the analysts have to agree and to 80% when more than half have to (p. 138).

Observational studies came out less robust than experiments, both on the common scale, where 28% of the reanalyses of observational studies fell inside the region of ±0.05 d against 44% of those of experiments, and in their conclusions, where 69% of the reanalyses of observational studies reached the same conclusion as the original against 82% of those of experiments (pp. 137, 139). The workshop's Europeanisation case study is an observational study, and the Housing and racial bias case study an experiment. The same variability appears in large studies, since "studies with large sample sizes are not immune to analytical variability" (p. 137).

The authors draw two lessons from these results. They "caution against using blanket rules in aggregating or interpreting results across different analytical approaches within the same investigation" (p. 141), and they argue that "[w]ithout exploring this variability, authors cannot guarantee consumers of their research that the reported conclusions hold a privileged status over alternative conclusions" (p. 140). On the scale itself, the article points to the recent proposal of 'generalized marginal effects', an effect size metric "that is both formally applicable and comparable across different statistical models" (p. 138), which it had not planned to compute from the start.

### Reading a converted effect size {#sec-reading}

Each converted effect size in the record therefore carries a history of choices, some made by the analyst and some by the conversion, and a reader of the article has to reconstruct that history before comparing two of them. The workshop's meta-analysis modules reconstruct it for the five analysts of each case study, and the same points can be checked for any reanalysis:

- which number of units entered the conversion: the residual degrees of freedom of a fixed-effects model, an approximation such as that of Satterthwaite, or the count of respondents standing in for degrees of freedom that the software did not report;
- whether the reported statistic carries a sign at all, since a chi-square does not, and how the sign in the record was set;
- which decisions the instruction of the second task fixed, and which it left to the analyst;
- in which figures of the article the study appears, since the article "could not determine the original effect size because of missing information" for five studies (p. 137), among them the paper of the Europeanisation case study, which therefore counts for the conclusions but for no comparison with an original effect size;
- and whether the conclusions and the effect sizes agree, since a claim can be upheld by every one of its analysts in the first task while their results spread widely on the common scale, as the Europeanisation claim was.

Each case study takes these points to its own five analysts in a module of its own. [Meta-analysis](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-housing/companion/meta-analysis.html) on the Housing site adds what a pooled estimate can say about the original experiment and its replication with new data. [Meta-analysis](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-eu/companion/meta-analysis.html) on the Europeanisation site sets the five analyses of one body of data beside the evidence that each of the 27 countries holds about the claim, and argues that the first of these comparisons needs a summary of a different kind from the second.

## The case studies in the record {#sec-cases}

The record of the programme differs from one case study to the next. The table gives, for each claim, the outcome of the reproduction and of the replication, and the conclusions that the five analysts of the robustness study reached in the first task.

| Case study | Original study | Reproduction | Robustness | Replication |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| [Housing and racial bias](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-housing/) | a field experiment in the *American Journal of Political Science* [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect] | never attempted, although the data and code are public | three of the five analysts found evidence for the claim, two evidence neither way | a new preregistered experiment with 3,050 housing authorities found no significant gap |
| [Europeanisation and the economy](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-eu/) | an analysis of Eurobarometer surveys in the *European Sociological Review* [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic] | two attempts from the original materials, neither successful | all five found evidence for the claim | judged not successful on later Eurobarometer waves |

Read across the rows, the three kinds of repetition do not move together. The Europeanisation claim, which every analyst upheld in the first task, could be neither reproduced from its original materials nor replicated on later waves of its survey, while the Housing claim, which three of its five analysts upheld, did not replicate in a new experiment, and SCORE never attempted to reproduce the paper, although its data and code are public. Two case studies are far too few for a conclusion about the literature, but they show, case by case, why the workshop keeps the three questions apart, and each case-study site tells the story of its own row on its background page.

## The workshop's exercise {#sec-course}

The workshop's exercise repeats the design of the robustness study with the class in the place of its analysts. Each participant receives the claim and the data of a case study, writes an estimand statement, which names the quantity that an analysis of the claim should estimate, and reproduces the result recorded in the robustness study for one of the five analysts of the case study, from the data behind it. In the formats that take the exercise further, the participant then works through the decisions that lie between the data and a result, declares one specification in a short preregistration before running it, and sends the result to a class chart, on which it sits beside the results of the rest of the class, those of the five analysts and the curve of the claim, so that each participant becomes a sixth analyst of the claim. Each case study closes on its replication, which asks what new data add to what the reanalyses showed. The meta-analysis modules of the case-study sites build on the [common scale](#sec-scale) of the robustness study.
